claims.text: The baseline uses FeCoNiCrAl powder with a particle-size range of 15–45 μm.
Coatings produced from the 15–45 μm feedstock under the baseline conditions have insufficient coating thickness.
The proposed single intervention is to increase the powder mass feed rate while holding the other spray parameters constant.
Increasing powder feed rate increases the coating deposition rate.
Increasing powder feed rate enhances splat overlap.
Enhanced splat overlap produces a denser and more continuous deposit.
The increased deposition rate permits a target coating thickness to be built in fewer spray passes.
Increasing feed rate reduces the high-temperature exposure time of individual particles.
Reduced high-temperature particle exposure minimizes in-flight oxidation.
High temperature and oxygen exposure during thermal spraying promote in-flight oxidation of HEA powder.
Atmospheric plasma spraying is applicable to deposition of an FeCoNiCrAl-family HEA coating.
An inert atmosphere and controlled spray distance can keep in-flight heating and oxidation minimal during atmospheric plasma spraying.
The increased-feed-rate coating will attain the thickness required for service as a TBC bond coat.
The increased-feed-rate coating will have as-sprayed oxidation comparable to the standard-feed-rate coating.
The increased-feed-rate coating will retain intact microstructure and acceptable splat morphology.
The intervention remains effective only below feed rates that cause agglomeration, poor splat formation, excessive thermal loading, splashing, or coating nonuniformity.

contradictions.description: The 15–45 μm value is introduced as the feedstock particle-size range but is later called the baseline coating thickness. No baseline coating-thickness value is actually provided.

The conditions call for an inert atmosphere during atmospheric plasma spraying, while the intervention only holds carrier-gas composition constant and does not specify an inert chamber or shielding method. Thus the claimed inert operating environment is not operationally reconciled with the atmospheric process.
